exercise1.prompt: The seven days of the week, stored in whichever structure fits data that never changes

cases.name: the days are kept in a tuple, not a list
cases.call: [type(v).__name__ for v in list(globals().values()) if isinstance(v, (list, tuple, set)) and len(v) == 7]

hiddenCases.name: all seven days, in order
hiddenCases.call: [list(v) for v in list(globals().values()) if isinstance(v, tuple) and len(v) == 7]

exercise1.hint: The exercise never asks you to add a day or take one away, and the hint on the page is asking you to notice that. Pick the structure whose punctuation says the data is fixed.

exercise2.prompt: Count each word in ["apple", "banana", "apple", "cherry", "banana", "apple"] into a dictionary

cases.name: every word counted
cases.call: [v for v in list(globals().values()) if isinstance(v, dict) and 'apple' in v]

cases.name: the counts come out of a loop
cases.describe: a loop over the words, rather than three counts typed in by hand

hiddenCases.name: the six words from the exercise are the ones counted
hiddenCases.call: [len(v) for v in list(globals().values()) if isinstance(v, list) and 'apple' in v]

exercise2.hint: The first time you meet a word there is no count to add to yet, so the two cases are different: start it at 1, or add 1 to what is already there. Deciding which is what the `if` is for.

questions.prompt: Match each job to the structure that fits it best.
left: A to-do list you keep adding to
The seven days of the week
Looking a phone number up by name
The unique visitors to a site
questions.explain: Order plus change means a list, fixed order means a tuple, lookup by label means a dictionary, and uniqueness means a set.

questions.prompt: You need to check, many times, whether a username has been taken. Which structure?
questions.explain: A set answers `in` without walking every item, and taken usernames are unique anyway, so nothing is lost by dropping the order.

questions.prompt: What is the shape of a word-count result?
choices: A dictionary of word to count
questions.explain: Every count belongs to a word, and a dictionary is what ties one value to one label. A list of counts would lose which word each belonged to.

questions.prompt: Which questions actually decide which structure to use?
choices: Does the order of the items matter?
Will the data change after it is created?
Do I look things up by position or by label?
Which one has the shortest name?
questions.explain: Order, mutability and how you look things up are the three that separate the four structures. Everything else is preference.
